site.title: Which AI Model? — a portfolio project by Saber Sojudi
site.description: Five AI tools moved onto one shared foundation, then seven models tested on real customer messages for quality, cost and speed. Results, a decision picker and the limits, stated plainly.

hero.lead: I moved five scattered AI tools onto one shared foundation, then tested which AI model does each job best for the money. The whole benchmark ran on real customer messages, and every number here is rebuilt from the committed results.
hero.fine: Independent project. Public datasets only. No employer or client is named anywhere on this page.
hero.example_legend: Each row is one model answering the same message. ✓ means the intent matched; time and cost are that single recorded call.
hero.example_source_suffix: shown exactly as the model saw it.
hero.example_note: The dataset is public, so a model may have seen this message during training. That is a limit of public benchmarks, not a hidden advantage: all seven models saw the same text.

numbers.title: What the benchmark found
numbers.lead: Every value below is copied from a committed file under results/ and names that file in the technical details.
numbers.baseline_lead: A word-count model (TF-IDF plus logistic regression) trained on the public training split. It costs nothing and needs no API.
numbers.baseline_note: The models still beat it, but not by a landslide. Any claimed AI win has to clear this line.

picker.title: Pick a model for the job
picker.lead: A model is good enough when it is within three points of the best model on that task. The picker then chooses the cheapest, the most accurate or the fastest good-enough model. Ties go to the lower cost.

before_after.title: One tool, two wirings
before_after.lead: The router used to call a provider directly: a raw HTTP request, a key read from the environment, and a label pulled out of free text. The migrated version asks for a typed schema through the shared layer and never parses free text.
before_after.lines_title: Lines are not the whole story
before_after.lines_lead: Raw lines went up, because every function is typed and documented. The tool's own logic moved into a shared frame, so what each tool owns is now a schema, a prompt and two small functions.
before_after.lines_source: Counts and source hashes are recorded in results/inventory/migration.json.
before_after.inventory_lead: A static scanner reads the code and lists every place a model is called. The before column is five different wirings; the after column is two shared call sites for the same five jobs.
before_after.inventory_after_note: The other three tools now run through the same shared module, so the scanner sees two call sites instead of five.

gate.title: A cheaper model is not automatically a safe swap
gate.lead: The regression gate compares a candidate model with the current baseline. It blocks a change when any task drops more than the point limit, or when structured replies fall below the schema-valid floor, or when the runs are not comparable at all.
gate.refusal_title: A refusal is never a pass
gate.refusal_body: Two fixture runs with the same metrics but a different prompt version were refused before any comparison. An incomparable run cannot silently pass the gate.

docs.title: It answers with citations, or it says it does not know
docs.lead: The docs assistant retrieves passages from this project's own guide and must cite the ids it used. These three answers are recorded from the live run, not rewritten for the page.

v11.title: Your own task: test it, re-test it
v11.lead: The four tasks above are fixed benchmarks. This one is the template for your own: one specification file plus one labelled data file, no Python. It is T-DEFECT, sorting public vehicle-owner complaints into component groups and flagging the safety-relevant ones.
v11.defect_sample_note: 600 items, sampled from public NHTSA complaints. Gemini 4 Argon was scored on 400 of them after the budget cut, so its interval is wider.
v11.defect_source_note: Every row is a committed cell in results/runs/live-v1.1/cells.json; the baseline is results/baseline/defect.json. No model was called to build this page.
v11.floor_rule_suffix: safety recall on this task is never recommended, whatever its group accuracy.
v11.recheck_title: When a new model comes out
v11.recheck_lead: A benchmark result is about one model, at one moment, with one prompt and one set of settings. When any of those changes, re-test instead of trusting the old number. These are the exact commands from docs/recheck.md.

steps.title: A new model came out
steps.body: A new model has no earlier answers, so a normal record run is enough: only the new model's calls are made. Then gate it against the committed run.

commands.text:
wam bench --mode record --models config/new-model.lock.toml \
  --tasks T-SCOPE --run-id new-model

commands.note: Then compare it with the committed run:

steps.title: The same model id behaves differently
steps.body: This is what re-check is for. It records fresh answers, never reuses a saved one, scores them, and gates them against the earlier run with the same model id on both sides.

commands.text:
wam recheck run \
  --models config/models.lock.toml \
  --tasks T-SCOPE \
  --against results/runs/live \
  --candidate gpt-6-luna \
  --run-id recheck-gpt-6-luna

steps.title: You changed a setting
steps.body: Temperature, reasoning and the output allowance are recorded in the run manifest. A difference is refused unless you say it was intended; then the gate returns its normal verdict plus a WARN line naming every difference.

commands.text:
wam recheck run \
  --models config/models.lock.toml \
  --tasks T-SCOPE \
  --against results/runs/live \
  --candidate gpt-6-luna \
  --accept-settings-mismatch \
  --run-id recheck-gpt-6-luna-warm

v11.demo_title: The re-check demo, as it ran
v11.demo_lead: GPT 6 Luna on T-SCOPE, recorded fresh at temperature 0 and gated against the committed v1 run.
v11.demo_note: The demo answers are committed under recordings/fresh/recheck-demo/, so make all replays them with no network call and no cost.
v11.volume_title: What it costs at your volume
v11.volume_lead: Cost is linear from the measured cost per 1,000 items: cost per month = cost per 1,000 × items per month ÷ 1,000. There are no volume discounts and no other extrapolation.
v11.volume_hint: Type a volume and the last column recalculates in the browser.
v11.volume_no_js: Without JavaScript the three fixed volumes still show the same arithmetic in the static table.
v11.volume_price_note: Prices as of 29 October 2026, from the committed price table; a later price change is not reflected.
v11.volume_unknown: An unknown measured cost stays unknown.
v11.cards_lead: Every card states the job, the data, the results, the recommendation, the gate rule, the exact re-check command and the monthly cost.

limits.title: What this benchmark does not prove
limits.lead: Read these before quoting a number.
items: All seven models were reached through one gateway (OpenCode Go), each in its lab's own API format. Other providers' direct endpoints were tested only with mocks.
Four of the five before tools were written for this project. Only the tool-calling agent is adapted from real earlier code, and it is credited in THIRD_PARTY.md.
Tiers are mixed on purpose: Gemini 4 Argon is a flagship, the other six are small models. A flagship winning on quality is expected; the useful question is what the small models cost.
The datasets are public, so models may already know some test messages. All seven saw the same text, so the comparison is still like for like, but absolute scores may be optimistic.
The structured-reply sample is a subset of the routing sample, so the recorded answers are not independent questions.
The gateway did not send measured cost on every model. Where it did not, the committed price table is used, and the measured-versus-list gap is computed only over models that have both.
Results and prices are dated in the technical details below. A later price change is not reflected here.
The docs task was scored with an in-memory index built from the same guide and the same pinned embeddings as the pgvector store. Retrieval ids matched pgvector on every gold question.

technical.title: How it was built and how to reproduce it
technical.summary: Fixed samples, versioned prompts and deterministic scoring make the recorded comparisons reproducible. No model judged another model.
stack: Python 3.12, uv, Ruff, strict mypy, pytest
LangChain v1 and LangGraph v1 for the shared model layer
Pydantic schemas for every structured output
Postgres with pgvector for the docs index
A local JSONL trace for every model call; no hosted tracing required
Committed recordings replayed by make all, with no key and no network
data: Banking77 (PolyAI) — routing and structured replies, CC-BY-4.0
The project guide in docs/guide — written for this repository, MIT
technical.reproduce_body: Clone the repository, run make all, and open dist/which-ai-model/index.html. Replay uses the committed recordings: no API key, no paid call, no network. The live run is the only step that ever spent money.
technical.results_lead: Every model on every task, with the primary metric, cost per 1,000 items and median latency.
